brief.goal: Find up to four checked supporting publications for the exact chosen hook: Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?
brief.output: Checked supporting source cards with title, publisher, date, lesson, species, region, limits and 1-4 facts per card, each with a short exact quote. Maximum 25 quoted words total per publication. Identify unresolved necessary gaps. No scripts or replacement hooks.
questions: What is a cockroach egg case, what does it enclose, and where do American cockroaches deposit it around buildings? Establish the setting without generalizing to every cockroach species.

How does Evania appendigaster place its egg inside the case, and what documented sequence follows through larval feeding, pupation and adult emergence? Clarify the fate of the cockroach eggs without assuming every attack succeeds.
Which visible features help explain what an ensign wasp is and distinguish the adult from its developing larva? Verify the characteristic body shape and movements before describing them.
Which cockroach species are documented hosts, and what evidence establishes relevance to Texas homes? Keep general biology separate from any location-specific measurements.

What can a homeowner reasonably infer from finding an adult ensign wasp indoors, and what observations would help assess cockroach activity? Establish why a sighting alone cannot locate an egg case, confirm an active infestation or demonstrate complete control.
scope_constraints: Use primary research or university extension pages on these domains: citybugs.tamu.edu, fireant.tamu.edu, extensionentomology.tamu.edu, agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, npic.orst.edu, epa.gov, ars.usda.gov, extension.msstate.edu, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, academic.oup.com, extension.okstate.edu, fireants.tennessee.edu
Use public search and original readable pages; no snippets as evidence, paid fallback, model calls, cookies, new logins or browser.
Keep the exact selected hook and one coherent lesson. Explain species names in plain speech. No em dashes in authored prose.
Limit conclusions to documented species and evidence. Do not infer active infestation, location of an egg case or complete pest control from one adult wasp sighting.
No pesticide prescriptions, dosing, medical advice or invented behavior.
Main publication already checked: https://citybugs.tamu.edu/2015/05/05/flag-waving-for-americans/ . Read for context; do not return it as new supporting evidence.
Research only relevant gaps. State limits where no local measurement exists. Stop after enough evidence for the lesson.

In general, the evolution of scale insects seems to show multiple cyclic conversions from oviparous reproduction to ovoviviparous/viviparous reproduction with the emergence of new peculiar adaptations for eggs’ protection (Fig. 7).
According to this hypothesis, most common reasons for the obligate egg retention are different variants of paedogenesis and neoteny, when the reproducing larva or nymph has lost special adult structures responsible for oviposition, with quick passage of the egg through the oviducts and fertilization of the egg in ectodermal parts of the oviduct
A similar situation also occurs in the cases of different morphological or physiological transformations, which are related not with paedogenesis, but with changes in the imaginal reproductive system.

This synchronization of hatching, enabling the eggs to emerge from diapause in the spring, could be considered an evolutionary adaptation aimed at postponing hatching of late-spawned eggs until a time allowing for completion of the full development cycle, including the parasitic larval stage.
About 3 weeks after the eggs were laid, fully developed larvae could be seen under the egg integuments, and some of them made small movements. In another case, where 14 batches of eggs were laid by five females in the spring or early summer, the larvae hatched when they were fully developed.
Only the winter temperature of 4 °C increased the hatching percentage, the intermediate temperature (10 °C) had the same effect as 20 °C.
According to Martin (2010), temperature stimulates eggs to emerge from diapause in water mites inhabiting springs and streams.
